text:
Ashwagandha Root

Ashwagandha root [Withania somnifera] is a foundational adaptogenic herb in Ayurvedic medicine, approved in the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia primarily for its adaptogenic, anti-stress, and immunomodulatory properties. Its principal bioactive constituents — the steroidal lactones known as withanolides — are understood to modulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, reduce cortisol levels, and exert anxiolytic effects partly via GABAergic pathways. Clinical trials support its use in reducing perceived stress and anxiety, improving physical endurance and muscular recovery, and enhancing cognitive function including memory and reaction time. Evidence also suggests benefits in thyroid function support, male reproductive health (spermatogenesis and testosterone levels), and adjunctive oncology support, though larger randomized controlled trials are warranted for several indications.

Preparation: Dried root powder: 3–6 g per day in divided doses, typically taken with warm milk or water. Standardized extract (1.5–5% withanolides): 300–600 mg per day in divided doses. Tincture (1:5, 60% ethanol): 6–12 mL per day. Decoction: 1–2 teaspoons of root powder simmered in 8 oz water or milk for 15 minutes, taken once or twice daily. Preparations are generally taken for a minimum of 4–8 weeks to assess therapeutic effect.
Indication: Primary indications: stress and anxiety [adaptogenic use], fatigue and debility, cognitive decline, immune dysfunction, male infertility and low testosterone, thyroid hypofunction, and adjunctive support in oncology. Secondary indications include insomnia, inflammatory conditions, and athletic performance enhancement.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera). Part used: Root. Key active compounds: withanolides (steroidal lactones, standardized extracts typically 1.5–5% withanolides), alkaloids (withanine, somniferine), saponins (sitoindosides VII–X), iron, and withaferins.
title: Ashwagandha Root

text:
Astragalus Root

Astragalus root [Radix Astragali; Huang Qi] is an adaptogenic and immunomodulatory herb drawn from traditional Chinese medicine and formally assessed in the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia monograph. Its principal constituents — polysaccharides [astragalans], triterpenoid saponins [astragalosides], and isoflavonoid flavonoids — collectively enhance innate and adaptive immune function by stimulating macrophage activity, promoting T-cell proliferation, and upregulating cytokine production including interferon-gamma and interleukin-2. Clinical and preclinical evidence supports its use as an adjunct in cancer-related immunosuppression, chronic fatigue, and recurrent upper respiratory infections, with several controlled trials demonstrating reduced incidence and duration of common colds and improved quality-of-life markers in oncology patients receiving chemotherapy. The astragaloside IV fraction, and its aglycone cycloastragenol, has additionally attracted research interest for telomerase activation, though clinical evidence for anti-aging applications remains preliminary.

Preparation: Dried root (decoction): 9–30 g daily in divided doses, simmered in water for 20–45 minutes. Standardized extract (capsule/tablet): 250–500 mg two to three times daily, standardized to ≥ 0.4% astragalosides or ≥ 40% polysaccharides. Tincture (1:5, 30% ethanol): 3–5 mL three times daily. Use is typically sustained over weeks to months as a tonic [fu zheng] course; short-term acute use is not the primary indication per the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia monograph.
Indication: Immune deficiency and immunosuppression (including chemotherapy adjunct); recurrent upper respiratory tract infections; chronic fatigue; adaptogenic tonic support.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Astragalus (Astragalus membranaceus). Part used: Root. Key active compounds include polysaccharides (astragalans), saponins (astragalosides I–IV, including cycloastragenol), and flavonoids (calycosin, formononetin); standardized extracts may specify polysaccharide content ≥ 40% or astragaloside IV ≥ 0.04%.
title: Astragalus Root

text:
Black Cohosh

Black cohosh (Actaea racemosa) root and rhizome are primarily indicated for the relief of menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, night sweats, mood disturbances, and sleep disruption, and are also used for premenstrual syndrome and dysmenorrhea [painful menstruation]. Its mechanism of action remains under investigation; earlier hypotheses of estrogenic activity via isoflavone content have largely been refuted, with current evidence suggesting selective serotonergic and dopaminergic receptor modulation by triterpene glycosides as a more plausible pathway. Multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses — most prominently those evaluating the proprietary extract Remifemin — have demonstrated statistically significant reductions in the Kupperman Menopausal Index and vasomotor symptom frequency compared to placebo, though effect sizes are moderate and long-term safety beyond six months requires further study. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes the root and rhizome as meeting established quality standards when triterpene glycoside content is verified by HPLC.

Preparation: Dried root and rhizome: 40–200 mg/day as crude drug. Standardized dry extract (standardized to ≥1% triterpene glycosides as 27-deoxyactein): 20–40 mg twice daily (equivalent to the Remifemin dosing protocol). Liquid extract (1:1 in 60% ethanol): 0.3–2 mL/day. Tincture (1:5 in 60% ethanol): 2–4 mL/day. Duration of use: AHP and Commission E recommend reassessment after 6 months of continuous use pending further long-term safety data, particularly regarding hepatotoxicity signals identified in post-market surveillance.
Indication: Menopausal vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats); premenstrual syndrome (PMS); dysmenorrhea [painful menstruation]; mood and sleep disturbances associated with perimenopause.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Black cohosh AHP (Actaea racemosa, syn. Cimicifuga racemosa). Part used: Root and rhizome. Key active compounds: triterpene glycosides (primarily actein and 27-deoxyactein, standardized to ≥1% triterpene glycosides calculated as 27-deoxyactein), isoflavones (formerly characterized; now considered absent or trace), and resinous constituents including cimicifugin.
title: Black Cohosh

text:
California Poppy

California poppy (Eschscholzia californica) is used therapeutically as a mild sedative, anxiolytic [anxiety-reducing], and analgesic [pain-relieving] agent, with traditional and emerging clinical application for insomnia, nervous tension, and mild pain. Its primary mechanism of action is attributed to isoquinoline alkaloids — particularly californidine and eschscholtzine — which are thought to interact with GABA-ergic [gamma-aminobutyric acid] pathways and opioid receptors, though the plant does not contain morphine or codeine and is not pharmacologically equivalent to the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum). Preclinical studies support anxiolytic and sedative effects in animal models, and limited human clinical data suggest benefit for sleep quality and anxiety, though large randomized controlled trials are lacking. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes its use as a gentle nervine [nerve-calming agent] suitable for mild to moderate presentations.

Preparation: Dried aerial parts: 2–4 g as a tea (infusion or decoction) up to three times daily. Fluid extract (1:1 in 25% ethanol): 2–4 mL up to three times daily. Tincture (1:5 in 40–50% ethanol): 2–4 mL up to three times daily. Standardized extracts: per manufacturer's specifications, typically standardized to total alkaloid content. Not recommended during pregnancy without professional supervision.
Indication: Insomnia, anxiety, nervous tension, mild pain, nervous excitability in children (at reduced doses under supervision)

Original: Eschscholzia californica — aerial parts. Active constituents include isoquinoline alkaloids (californidine, eschscholtzine, protopine, allocryptopine, and sanguinarine), flavone glycosides (including rutin), and carotenoid pigments. Alkaloid content is not standardized to a fixed percentage in current AHP guidelines.
title: California Poppy

text:
Cannabis (Marijuana) Flower

Cannabis flower is used therapeutically for pain management, nausea and vomiting associated with chemotherapy, appetite stimulation in wasting conditions, and muscle spasticity, primarily through modulation of the endocannabinoid system via CB1 and CB2 receptor agonism. The principal psychoactive constituent, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol [THC], mediates analgesia, antiemesis, and appetite stimulation centrally and peripherally, while cannabidiol [CBD] contributes anti-inflammatory, anxiolytic, and neuroprotective effects with minimal psychoactivity. Clinical evidence from randomized controlled trials supports efficacy for chemotherapy-induced nausea, neuropathic pain, and spasticity in multiple sclerosis; evidence for other indications remains preliminary. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia monograph establishes identity, purity, and quality standards to ensure consistent therapeutic application across variable chemotypes.

Original: Cannabis sativa L., Family Cannabaceae. Part used: Flower (inflorescence). Primary active constituents: delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), cannabidiol (CBD), cannabigerol (CBG), terpenes (myrcene, limonene, beta-caryophyllene), and flavonoids. THC content variable by chemotype; CBD:THC ratios define chemotypic classification per AHP standards.
title: Cannabis (Marijuana) Flower

text:
Narrow-Leaved Coneflower (Echinacea angustifolia) Root

Echinacea angustifolia root is used primarily as an immunomodulator [immune-system modifier] for the prevention and symptomatic treatment of upper respiratory tract infections, including the common cold and influenza-like illnesses. Its principal mechanism of action involves stimulation of phagocytosis [engulfment of pathogens by immune cells], activation of macrophages and natural killer cells, and modulation of cytokine [cell-signaling protein] production, largely attributed to its alkylamide and polysaccharide constituents. Alkylamides are thought to bind to cannabinoid receptor type 2 (CB2), contributing to anti-inflammatory effects. Clinical evidence, while variable across preparations and species, generally supports modest reduction in duration and severity of cold symptoms when treatment is initiated at early onset, with some evidence for prophylactic [preventive] use during periods of elevated exposure risk.

Preparation: Per American Herbal Pharmacopoeia guidelines: (1) Dried root — 1–3 g as decoction [root simmered in water] three times daily; (2) Tincture (1:5, 60% ethanol) — 3–5 mL three times daily; (3) Fluid extract (1:1) — 1–2 mL three times daily; (4) Standardized solid-dose extract — per manufacturer specification, typically standardized to alkylamide or echinacoside content. Short-term use (up to 10 days for acute illness) is standard; extended prophylactic courses up to 8 weeks have been studied. Not generally recommended for continuous use beyond 8 weeks without guidance.
Indication: Upper respiratory tract infections (common cold, influenza-like illness); immune system support; prophylaxis during high-risk exposure periods

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Echinacea angustifolia AHP (Echinacea angustifolia). Part used: Root. Key active compounds include alkylamides (isobutylamides), caffeic acid derivatives (echinacoside, cynarin, cichoric acid), polysaccharides, and glycoproteins.
title: Narrow-Leaved Coneflower (Echinacea angustifolia) Root

text:
Elderberry

Elderberry fruit [Sambucus nigra fructus] is primarily indicated for the prevention and symptomatic treatment of upper respiratory viral infections, including influenza A and B and the common cold. Its antiviral mechanism is attributed chiefly to anthocyanin-rich polyphenols that are understood to bind viral surface hemagglutinin proteins, thereby inhibiting host-cell attachment and replication, while simultaneously stimulating pro-inflammatory cytokine production to enhance immune response. Clinical evidence from randomized controlled trials supports a reduction in influenza symptom duration and severity when elderberry extract is administered within 24–48 hours of symptom onset; a 2016 randomized trial (Tiralongo et al.) demonstrated significant reduction in cold duration and severity among air travelers. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia [AHP] recognizes the fruit as having a well-documented, if still evolving, evidence base for immunomodulatory and antiviral applications.

Preparation: Standardized liquid extract or syrup (typically standardized to anthocyanin content): 15 mL of syrup (containing approximately 3.8 g of extract) four times daily for 5 days during acute illness. Encapsulated dried extract: 300–500 mg two to three times daily. Decoction of dried berries: 5–10 g of dried fruit per cup, simmered 10–15 minutes, two to three cups daily. Lozenges and tinctures are also commercially available; doses should align with AHP-recognized standardized anthocyanin levels where possible. Raw or unripe berries should not be consumed due to the presence of sambunigrin, a cyanogenic glycoside.
Indication: Influenza (types A and B); upper respiratory tract infections (common cold); immune support; antiviral prophylaxis

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Elderberry (Sambucus nigra). Part used: Fruit. Key active compounds include anthocyanins (principally cyanidin-3-glucoside and cyanidin-3-sambubioside), flavonoids (quercetin, rutin, isoquercitrin), polyphenols, lectins, and viburnic acid.
title: Elderberry

text:
American Ginseng Root

American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius) root is a well-characterized [adaptogen] used primarily to support cognitive function, moderate stress responses, and regulate blood glucose levels, particularly in individuals with type 2 diabetes. Its principal bioactive constituents—the ginsenosides—are triterpenoid saponins that modulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, exhibit antioxidant activity, and interact with insulin signaling pathways. Clinical trials have demonstrated statistically significant reductions in postprandial blood glucose in both diabetic and healthy subjects, and preliminary evidence supports improvements in working memory and immune resilience. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes it as distinct from Asian ginseng (Panax ginseng) in its ginsenoside profile and considers it generally milder in stimulant effect.

Preparation: Dried root: 1–2 g per day as decoction or in capsule/tablet form. Standardized extract: 200–400 mg per day standardized to ≥4–8% ginsenosides. Tincture (1:5, 40–60% ethanol): 3–5 mL up to three times daily. Best taken 30–40 minutes before meals when used for glycemic support. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia advises a minimum 6–8 week course for adaptogenic indications.
Indication: Primary indications: glycemic regulation (postprandial blood glucose reduction in type 2 diabetes); cognitive support (working memory, mental fatigue); immune modulation; general adaptogenic use (stress resilience and physical performance).

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Ginseng American (Panax quinquefolius). Part used: Root. Key active compounds: ginsenosides (protopanaxadiol and protopanaxatriol saponins, typically 4–8% total ginsenosides by dry weight), polysaccharides, and polyacetylenes.
title: American Ginseng Root

text:
Maitake Mushroom

Maitake mushroom (Grifola frondosa) is used primarily as an immunomodulatory agent, with its principal bioactive constituents—beta-1,3/1,6-glucans, particularly the proprietary D-fraction extract—shown to stimulate macrophage, natural killer (NK) cell, and T-lymphocyte activity via binding to pattern-recognition receptors (notably Dectin-1 and complement receptor 3). The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes its application in supporting immune function, as an adjunct in oncology care [specifically in reducing immunosuppression associated with conventional chemotherapy], and in the management of metabolic conditions including type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Clinical evidence includes preliminary human trials and robust in vitro and animal data supporting antitumor and hypoglycemic effects, though large-scale randomized controlled trials in humans remain limited. The fruiting body and its standardized extracts are considered generally safe for long-term use at recommended doses.

Preparation: Dried fruiting body powder: 3–7 g per day in divided doses, typically encapsulated or as tea/decoction. Standardized D-fraction liquid extract: 0.5–1 mg per kg body weight per day (as beta-glucan equivalent), often taken in divided doses before meals. Hot-water or hot-water/ethanol dual extracts are the pharmacopoeially preferred preparation methods to maximize polysaccharide and triterpene extraction. Tinctures (1:5 in 25–40% ethanol) are also used though considered less optimal for polysaccharide delivery.
Indication: Primary indications: immune system support; adjunct therapy in cancer care (reducing chemotherapy-related immunosuppression); management of type 2 diabetes (glycemic support); hypertension; hypercholesterolemia.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Maitake mushroom (Grifola frondosa). Part used: Fruiting body. Key active compounds: beta-1,3/1,6-glucans (notably the D-fraction polysaccharide complex); also contains ergosterol (provitamin D2 precursor), phospholipids, and various amino acids. Polysaccharide content variable by preparation; standardized D-fraction extracts typically 20–30% beta-glucan by weight.
title: Maitake Mushroom

text:
Reishi Mushroom

Reishi mushroom [Ganoderma lucidum] fruiting body is used principally as an immunomodulatory and adaptogenic agent, with applications in supporting immune function, managing fatigue, and as an adjunct in oncology care. Its primary mechanisms of action involve beta-glucan-mediated activation of macrophages, natural killer cells, and dendritic cells, while triterpenes (ganoderic acids) exert anti-inflammatory effects through inhibition of histamine release and modulation of arachidonic acid pathways. Clinical evidence supports modest improvements in fatigue and quality-of-life measures in cancer patients receiving conventional therapy, as well as beneficial effects on immune parameters; however, large-scale randomized controlled trials remain limited and most supporting data derive from in vitro, animal, and small human studies. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes Reishi as a Class 1 herb (safe for use when appropriately used), with quality standards specifying minimum thresholds for both polysaccharide and triterpene content to ensure therapeutic equivalence across preparations.

Preparation: Dried fruiting body (whole or powdered): 1.5–9 g per day in divided doses, typically prepared as a decocted tea (simmered 30–60 minutes) or taken as encapsulated powder. Standardized extract (polysaccharide ≥10%, triterpenes ≥4%): 150–900 mg per day in divided doses. Tincture (1:5, 40–60% ethanol): 1–2 mL three times daily. Dual-extraction products (aqueous + ethanolic) are preferred to capture both water-soluble beta-glucans and alcohol-soluble triterpenes. Duration of use: typically 8–12 weeks for immune support; longer-term use is considered safe under practitioner guidance.
Indication: Primary indications: immune system support and immunomodulation; cancer-related fatigue and quality-of-life improvement (adjunctive use alongside conventional oncology treatment); general adaptogenic support and stress resilience; mild hepatoprotection; supportive care in chronic fatigue and recurrent infection.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Reishi mushroom (Ganoderma lucidum). Part used: Fruiting body. Key active compounds: polysaccharides (beta-glucans, particularly beta-1,3/1,6-glucans; typically ≥10% in standardized extracts), triterpenes (ganoderic acids A–Z and related lanostane-type triterpenes; typically ≥4% in standardized extracts), ergosterol (provitamin D2 precursor), adenosine, and minor peptidoglycans and lectins.
title: Reishi Mushroom

text:
Rhodiola Root (Golden Root / Arctic Root)

Rhodiola rosea root is classified as an adaptogen [a substance that non-specifically increases resistance to physical, chemical, and biological stressors] and is approved in several European countries for the alleviation of symptoms of stress, including fatigue and a sense of weakness. Its primary mechanism of action is thought to involve modulation of stress-response pathways, including inhibition of monoamine oxidase (MAO-A and MAO-B), upregulation of serotonin and dopamine transport, and normalization of cortisol secretion via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Clinical trials — including randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies — have demonstrated statistically significant improvements in fatigue, cognitive performance, mental work capacity, and mood under conditions of stress-induced burnout, with a favorable tolerability and safety profile. The rosavins and salidroside are considered the primary bioactive markers, with salidroside exhibiting neuroprotective, antioxidant, and cardioprotective activities in preclinical models.

Original: Rhodiola rosea L. (Crassulaceae). Root and rhizome. Key active constituents: rosavins (rosavin, rosin, rosarin; standardized to ≥3%), salidroside (p-tyrosol glucoside; standardized to ≥1%), tyrosol, flavonoids (including rhodiolin, rhodionin, rhodiosin), organic acids, and monoterpenes (including rosiridol and rosaridin).
title: Rhodiola Root (Golden Root / Arctic Root)

text:
Shiitake Mushroom

Shiitake mushroom (Lentinula edodes) fruiting body is recognized for immunomodulatory, cardiovascular-supportive, and antimicrobial properties, with its primary active constituents being high-molecular-weight beta-glucans such as lentinan, which stimulate macrophage and natural killer cell activity. Eritadenine has been shown in preclinical studies to lower serum cholesterol by interfering with lipid metabolism, while ergosterol serves as a provitamin D2 precursor activated by ultraviolet light exposure. Clinical evidence supports modest immune enhancement in healthy adults and adjunctive use in oncology settings, though large-scale randomized controlled trials in humans remain limited. The antioxidant compound L-ergothioneine may contribute to cellular cytoprotection, and the overall safety profile of the fruiting body is well established at conventional dietary and supplemental doses.

Preparation: Dried fruiting body: 6–16 g/day as food or decoction. Standardized hot-water or hydroalcoholic extract (standardized to beta-glucan content): 1.5–3 g/day in divided doses. Capsules or tablets containing powdered fruiting body: per manufacturer's standardization, typically 500–1000 mg two to three times daily. Decoction: simmer 6–16 g dried mushroom in water for 20–30 minutes; consume 1–3 cups daily.
Indication: Primary indications: immune support and immunomodulation; adjunctive support in cancer care [lentinan fraction]; hypercholesterolemia and cardiovascular risk reduction; general adaptogenic and nutritive tonic use.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Shiitake mushroom (Lentinula edodes). Part used: Fruiting body. Key active compounds include beta-glucans (notably lentinan), eritadenine, polysaccharides, sterols (ergosterol/provitamin D2), and L-ergothioneine.
title: Shiitake Mushroom

text:
Wild Cherry Bark

Wild cherry bark (Prunus serotina) is used primarily as an antitussive [cough suppressant] and mild sedative for irritable, nonproductive coughs associated with respiratory tract conditions such as bronchitis and colds. Its principal mechanism of action involves the cyanogenic glycoside prunasin, which upon enzymatic hydrolysis releases hydrocyanic acid (HCN) in small quantities; HCN is thought to depress the cough reflex by acting on the sensory nerve endings in the respiratory mucosa and the medullary cough center. Tannins present in the bark contribute astringent and mild anti-inflammatory activity on mucous membranes. Clinical evidence is largely based on traditional and empirical use, with limited formal clinical trials; the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes its historical therapeutic application in Western herbalism for soothing bronchial irritation.

Preparation: Decoction: 1–2 g of dried bark per 150 mL water, taken up to three times daily. Fluid extract (1:1 in 25% ethanol): 1–2 mL up to three times daily. Tincture (1:5 in 40% ethanol): 2–4 mL up to three times daily. Dry extract in capsule or tablet form dosed to equivalent crude herb quantity. Note: preparations should be freshly prepared or properly dried and stored, as hydrocyanic acid content diminishes with age and improper storage; prolonged high-dose use is not recommended due to cyanogenic potential.
Indication: Primary indications: irritable and nonproductive cough; bronchial irritation; mild bronchitis; upper respiratory tract inflammation. Secondary: mild sedation, digestive astringency.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Wild cherry bark (Prunus serotina). Part used: Bark. Key active compounds include cyanogenic glycosides (principally prunasin), benzaldehyde, hydrocyanic acid (HCN) released upon hydrolysis, tannins, and flavonoids.
title: Wild Cherry Bark

text:
Wild Indigo Root

Wild indigo root (Baptisia tinctoria) is used primarily as an immunostimulant and antimicrobial agent, with traditional and contemporary applications in the management of upper respiratory tract infections, influenza-like illness, and recurrent infections associated with immune deficiency. Its mechanism of action is attributed chiefly to high-molecular-weight polysaccharides and isoflavonoid constituents that activate macrophages, stimulate lymphocyte proliferation, and enhance nonspecific immune response [immunomodulation]. Quinolizidine alkaloids, including cytisine and baptifoline, contribute antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties, though these compounds also account for the plant's relatively narrow therapeutic index and toxicity concerns at higher doses. Clinical evidence, though limited by small trial size, suggests benefit as an adjunct to Echinacea and Thuja in combination preparations for acute upper respiratory infections, where it appears to reduce symptom duration and severity.

Preparation: Per American Herbal Pharmacopoeia guidelines: Dried root decoction — 1–2 g per cup, up to three times daily; Fluid extract (1:1 in 60% ethanol) — 0.5–1 mL up to three times daily; Tincture (1:5 in 60% ethanol) — 1–2 mL up to three times daily. Most commonly used in standardized combination products (e.g., with Echinacea purpurea and Thuja occidentalis). Not recommended for long-term continuous use; typical course is 1–2 weeks for acute conditions.
Indication: Upper respiratory tract infections; influenza-like illness; immune deficiency with recurrent infections; adjunctive immunostimulation.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Wild indigo root (Baptisia tinctoria). Part used: Root. Key active compounds include quinolizidine alkaloids (cytisine, baptifoline, anagyrine), isoflavonoids (baptisin, pseudobaptigenin), and polysaccharides with immunostimulant activity.
title: Wild Indigo Root

text:
Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) — Aerial Parts

Yarrow (Achillea millefolium), used as dried aerial parts [herba millefolii], is pharmacopoeially recognized for its [antispasmodic], [anti-inflammatory], [diaphoretic], [astringent], and [bitter tonic] actions, with principal applications in functional gastrointestinal complaints (dyspepsia, bloating, mild gastrointestinal spasms) and febrile conditions requiring diaphoresis. Its anti-inflammatory activity is attributed primarily to chamazulene generated from the sesquiterpene lactone matricine during steam distillation of the essential oil, alongside flavonoid-mediated inhibition of cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways; achilleine is credited with hemostatic activity supporting topical use in minor wounds. Clinical evidence remains largely pre-clinical and pharmacological, with human trial data limited but consistent with traditional indications recognized by Commission E (Germany), ESCOP, and the World Health Organization; the herb is approved in several European national pharmacopoeias for loss of appetite and mild dyspeptic complaints. Topical application of the fresh herb or preparations thereof is also recognized for minor bleeding wounds and skin inflammation.

Preparation: Dried herb (infusion/tea): 2–4 g of dried aerial parts per 150 mL boiling water, steeped 10–15 minutes, taken 3× daily. Fluid extract (1:1 in 25% ethanol): 2–4 mL 3× daily. Tincture (1:5 in 45% ethanol): 3–5 mL 3× daily. Expressed juice of fresh plant: 5–10 mL 3× daily. Standardized dry extract: per manufacturer's specification, typically standardized to 0.02–0.05% total azulene or 0.2% apigenin-7-glucoside. External use: strong infusion or poultice of fresh/dried herb applied to wounds or inflamed skin as needed.
Indication: Functional dyspepsia; mild gastrointestinal spasms and bloating; loss of appetite (bitter tonic); febrile states requiring diaphoresis; minor wounds and superficial bleeding (topical hemostatic); mild inflammatory skin conditions (topical).

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Yarrow AHP (Achillea millefolium). Part used: Aerial parts (herb). Key active constituents include: volatile oils (0.2–1.0%), notably azulene (chamazulene) and camphor; sesquiterpene lactones (achillin, achillicin); flavonoids (apigenin, luteolin, rutin); alkaloids (achilleine, stachydrine); tannins; and bitter principles (achillic acid). The European Pharmacopoeia requires a minimum of 0.02% v/w of blue essential oil (calculated as azulene) and 0.2% total flavonoids (expressed as apigenin-7-glucoside).
title: Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) — Aerial Parts

text:
Yerba Mate

Yerba mate leaf is used primarily as a central nervous system [CNS] stimulant to temporarily relieve mental and physical fatigue, enhance alertness, and support thermogenic [heat-generating] metabolism. Its principal mechanism of action derives from caffeine and related xanthine alkaloids, which antagonize adenosine receptors in the brain, while the chlorogenic acids and flavonoids contribute antioxidant activity and may modulate glucose metabolism. Clinical and pharmacological evidence supports modest improvements in cognitive performance, sustained energy, and lipid metabolism, with some data suggesting benefit in weight management when combined with caloric restriction. The saponin fraction may contribute cholesterol-lowering effects, though robust randomized controlled trial evidence in humans remains limited for several of these indications.

Preparation: Dried leaf infusion (traditional 'mate' preparation): 3–10 g of dried leaf steeped in hot water (70–80°C, not boiling) for 3–5 minutes, consumed 1–3 times daily. Standardized dry extract capsules/tablets: typically 300–500 mg per dose, 1–3 times daily. Fluid extract (1:1): 3–5 mL up to three times daily. American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recommends avoiding prolonged very high-temperature infusions due to association with esophageal irritation risk.
Indication: Mental and physical fatigue; cognitive enhancement; thermogenic weight management support; mild diuresis; antioxidant support

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Yerba mate (Ilex paraguariensis). Part used: Leaf. Key active compounds include xanthine alkaloids (caffeine approximately 0.7–1.7%, theobromine approximately 0.3–0.9%, theophylline in minor amounts), chlorogenic acids (polyphenolic antioxidants), saponins (matesaponins), and flavonoids (quercetin, rutin, kaempferol).
title: Yerba Mate

text:
Yerba Santa

Yerba santa (Eriodictyon californicum) is a aromatic shrub native to the chaparral regions of California and northern Mexico, whose leaves have been used traditionally by Indigenous peoples and in American botanical medicine as a [expectorant] and [bronchodilator] for respiratory conditions. The leaf contains flavonoids—primarily [eriodictyol], [homoeriodictyol], and [chrysoeriol]—along with [resin acids] and volatile oils that are thought to account for its mucus-thinning and airway-relaxing properties. According to the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia, its primary approved therapeutic uses include relief of coughs, bronchitis, asthma, and hayfever, with eriodictyol demonstrating anti-inflammatory activity in preclinical studies; robust human clinical trial data remain limited. The herb is also applied topically as a poultice for bruises, insect bites, and minor wounds, consistent with its traditional [vulnerary] use.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Yerba santa (Eriodictyon californicum). Part used: Leaf.
title: Yerba Santa

text:
Usnea (Old Man's Beard Lichen)

Usnea barbata, commonly known as Old Man's Beard, is a lichen [composite organism: fungus + alga] whose thallus has been used traditionally as an [antimicrobial], [immunomodulatory], and [vulnerary] agent. The primary active constituent, usnic acid, exerts broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity—particularly against Gram-positive bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus spp.—by uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation in bacterial mitochondria, thereby disrupting ATP synthesis. Polysaccharide fractions contribute immunostimulant effects, stimulating macrophage activity and non-specific immune defenses, while mucilaginous components are thought to support demulcent action on mucous membranes of the respiratory and urinary tracts. Clinical evidence remains predominantly preclinical and traditional; robust human randomized controlled trials are limited, though in vitro and animal studies broadly support antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory claims recognized in the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia monograph.

Preparation: Dried thallus: 3–5 g daily as a decoction or cold infusion. Tincture (1:5, 25–40% ethanol): 3–5 mL three times daily. Fluid extract (1:1): 1–2 mL three times daily. Standardized solid extract (capsule or tablet): typically standardized to usnic acid content, per manufacturer's recommendation aligned with AHP dosing guidelines. Topical preparations: poultice or ointment of powdered thallus applied directly to wounds or skin infections as needed.
Indication: Primary indications: upper respiratory tract infections (including bronchitis and pharyngitis); urinary tract infections; superficial skin infections and wound healing; oral infections (as a topical rinse); general immune support.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Usnea (Usnea barbata). Part used: Lichen thallus. Key active compounds: usnic acid (primary constituent, typically 0.1–3% dry weight), polysaccharides (notably pustulan and isolichenan), phenolic depsides, and mucilaginous compounds.
title: Usnea (Old Man's Beard Lichen)

text:
Andrographis (King of Bitters)

Andrographis paniculata, commonly known as 'King of Bitters,' is a traditional Ayurvedic and Traditional Chinese Medicine herb whose aerial parts are used primarily for the prevention and symptomatic treatment of upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs), the common cold, and influenza-like illness. The primary active compounds, andrographolides [diterpene lactones], exert immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, and antiviral effects by stimulating innate immune responses, inhibiting NF-κB signaling, and suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokine production. Multiple randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews support its efficacy in reducing the severity and duration of uncomplicated URTIs, with evidence suggesting superiority over placebo and comparability to some conventional treatments. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes its use for mild-to-moderate infectious and inflammatory conditions, with a well-characterized safety profile at recommended doses.

Preparation: Dried herb (aerial parts): 3–6 g per day in divided doses, typically as decoction or tablet/capsule. Standardized extract (andrographolide ≥4–6%): 200–400 mg per day in divided doses. Hydroalcoholic tincture (1:5, 40–60% ethanol): 3–6 mL, three times daily. Treatment duration for acute URTI: 3–10 days per American Herbal Pharmacopoeia guidelines. Not recommended for use during pregnancy.
Indication: Upper respiratory tract infections (common cold, influenza-like illness); fever; immune support; mild inflammatory conditions

Original: Andrographis paniculata; aerial parts; key active constituents include andrographolides (diterpene lactones), notably andrographolide (the primary marker compound, standardized to ≥4–6% in commercial preparations), neoandrographolide, 14-deoxyandrographolide, and arabinogalactan polysaccharides.
title: Andrographis (King of Bitters)

text:
Bacopa (Water Hyssop)

Bacopa monnieri is an Ayurvedic adaptogenic herb [rasayana] principally indicated for cognitive enhancement, memory support, and reduction of anxiety. Its primary active constituents, the bacosides, are believed to facilitate synaptic transmission by enhancing kinase activity, neuronal protein synthesis, and antioxidant defenses in the hippocampus, thereby supporting memory consolidation and neuroprotection. Clinical trials — including randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies in healthy adults and older populations — have demonstrated statistically significant improvements in verbal learning, memory acquisition, and delayed recall following 8–12 weeks of standardized extract administration. Anxiolytic effects are attributed in part to modulation of the serotonergic and GABAergic systems, consistent with its traditional use as a nervine tonic.

Preparation: Standardized dry extract (20–55% bacosides by weight): 300–450 mg once daily with food. Whole dried herb powder: 5–10 g per day in divided doses, traditionally prepared as a decoction or taken with warm milk and ghee. Liquid extract (1:2): 5–12 mL per day in divided doses. A minimum treatment duration of 8–12 weeks is recommended to observe cognitive effects. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia advises consistent daily use rather than as-needed dosing.
Indication: Primary indications: age-related cognitive decline, memory impairment, learning and attention support, anxiety, stress adaptation [adaptogenic use]. Secondary indications in traditional Ayurvedic practice include epilepsy support and general neurological tonic use.

Original: Plant: Bacopa monnieri (Bacopa; also known as Brahmi). Part used: Aerial parts. Key active compounds: bacosides A and B (saponin glycosides, primary nootropic constituents), bacopasaponins, alkaloids (brahmine, herpestine), phytosterols, betulinic acid, and flavonoids (luteolin, apigenin). Bacoside content is typically standardized to 20–55% in commercial extracts.
title: Bacopa (Water Hyssop)

text:
Boswellia (Indian Frankincense) Resin

Boswellia serrata resin, standardized to boswellic acids, is used therapeutically as an anti-inflammatory agent for conditions including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis), and asthma. Its primary mechanism of action involves selective, non-redox inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX), thereby blocking leukotriene biosynthesis — a pathway distinct from that targeted by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which typically inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes. Clinical trials have demonstrated statistically significant reductions in joint pain and swelling in osteoarthritis patients, improvements in pulmonary function in asthma subjects, and induction of remission in some inflammatory bowel disease cases. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes standardized Boswellia extracts [Shallaki in Ayurvedic tradition] as having a well-supported evidence base, particularly for musculoskeletal and gastrointestinal inflammatory conditions.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Boswellia (Boswellia serrata). Part used: Resin. Key active compounds: boswellic acids (notably acetyl-11-keto-β-boswellic acid [AKBA] and 11-keto-β-boswellic acid [KBA]), comprising up to 30% of the resin by weight; also contains essential oils (terpenes, including α-thujene and p-cymene) and polysaccharides.
title: Boswellia (Indian Frankincense) Resin

text:
Cordyceps Mushroom

Cordyceps sinensis, a parasitic fungus traditionally harvested from the Tibetan Plateau, is used in the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia context primarily as an adaptogen and tonic to support respiratory function, physical endurance, immune modulation, and kidney and liver health [nephroprotective, hepatoprotective]. Its principal bioactive constituent, cordycepin [3'-deoxyadenosine], along with beta-glucan polysaccharides and adenosine, is understood to modulate immune cell activity, enhance cellular ATP production, and exert antioxidant effects, thereby supporting oxygen utilization and fatigue resistance. Clinical and preclinical evidence suggests benefits in reducing fatigue and improving aerobic capacity in elderly populations, with additional study supporting immunostimulatory and anti-inflammatory activity, though large-scale randomized controlled trials in healthy adults remain limited. The fruiting body preparation is distinguished from mycelium-only products, as the fruiting body contains the broadest and most concentrated profile of characteristic active compounds.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Cordyceps (Cordyceps sinensis). Part used: Fruiting body. Key active compounds: cordycepin (3'-deoxyadenosine), polysaccharides (beta-glucans), adenosine, ergosterol, cordycepic acid (D-mannitol), and cyclosporin-related cyclopeptides.
title: Cordyceps Mushroom

text:
Eleuthero (Siberian Ginseng) Root

Eleuthero root is classified as an [adaptogen], a substance that nonspecifically increases the body's resistance to physical, chemical, and biological stressors. Its principal constituents, the eleutherosides — particularly eleutheroside B (syringin) and eleutheroside E — are understood to modulate neuroendocrine and immune function, in part through influence on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and enhancement of natural killer (NK) cell activity. Clinical evidence, primarily from Russian and Central European research, supports its use in improving work capacity, reducing fatigue, and enhancing immunological resilience under conditions of stress, though many foundational studies have been criticized for methodological limitations by contemporary standards. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes eleuthero as a tonic [adaptogenic] herb indicated for short- to medium-term support of physical and mental performance, immune competence, and convalescence.

Original: Eleutherococcus senticosus (Rupr. & Maxim.) Maxim. — Root. Key active constituents: eleutherosides (designated A through M), notably eleutheroside B (syringin) and eleutheroside E (syringing); polysaccharides (eleutherans); lignans; and coumarins. Eleutheroside content of standardized preparations typically referenced to eleutheroside B and E.
title: Eleuthero (Siberian Ginseng) Root

text:
Holy Basil (Tulsi)

Holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum), commonly known as tulsi, is an Ayurvedic adaptogenic herb whose leaves contain key active constituents including eugenol, rosmarinic acid, ursolic acid, and volatile oils (including linalool, methyl eugenol, and caryophyllene), which collectively contribute to its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and immunomodulatory properties. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes tulsi as an [adaptogen] useful for managing stress, supporting cognitive function, and promoting general wellness, with its mechanisms of action attributed to modulation of cortisol levels, inhibition of COX enzymes, and free-radical scavenging activity. Clinical and preclinical evidence supports its use in reducing psychological and physiological stress responses, improving blood glucose regulation, and exerting cardioprotective effects, though large-scale randomized controlled trials in humans remain limited. Standard preparations include dried leaf powder, aqueous or ethanolic extracts, and teas, with typical doses ranging from 300–600 mg of standardized extract twice daily or 2–3 g of dried leaf as an infusion up to three times daily.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Holy basil tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum). Part used: Leaf.
title: Holy Basil (Tulsi)

text:
Lion's Mane Mushroom

Lion's mane mushroom (Hericium erinaceus) is recognized in the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia primarily for its [nootropic] and neuroprotective properties, with principal therapeutic applications in cognitive support, mild cognitive impairment, and digestive health. Its bioactive compounds — notably hericenones and erinacines — are documented to stimulate [Nerve Growth Factor (NGF)] synthesis, supporting neuronal maintenance, regeneration, and plasticity. Clinical evidence, while still emerging, includes randomized controlled trials (notably Mori et al., 2009) demonstrating statistically significant improvements in cognitive function scores in older adults with mild cognitive impairment compared to placebo over 16 weeks, with effects attenuating upon cessation. The fruiting body's beta-glucan polysaccharides additionally confer immunomodulatory activity, and preliminary evidence supports gastroprotective effects relevant to gastric mucosal integrity.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Lion's mane mushroom (Hericium erinaceus). Part used: Fruiting body. Key active compounds: hericenones (aromatic compounds from fruiting body), erinacines (diterpenes from mycelium), beta-glucan polysaccharides (reported at approximately 20–40% of dry weight in quality preparations), and minor sterols including ergosterol.
title: Lion's Mane Mushroom

text:
Morinda Root (Ba Ji Tian)

Morinda officinalis root, known in Traditional Chinese Medicine as Ba Ji Tian, is classified as a kidney [shen] yang tonic and is principally indicated for conditions attributed to kidney yang deficiency, including impotence, infertility, irregular menstruation, cold extremities, lower back pain, and urinary frequency. Its pharmacological activity is thought to derive primarily from its iridoid glycosides and fructooligosaccharides, which demonstrate adaptogenic, anti-inflammatory, and mild androgenic properties in preclinical studies, with the oligosaccharide fraction showing particular promise in supporting adrenocortical function and bone density. Clinical and experimental evidence suggests immunomodulatory effects and potential benefit in osteoporosis models, though large-scale randomized controlled trials in human populations remain limited. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia monograph supports its use consistent with traditional indications pending further clinical validation.

Preparation: Dried root decoction [tang]: 9–15 g per day in water, simmered 30–45 minutes, consumed in divided doses. Concentrated granule extracts: dose adjusted by extraction ratio per manufacturer. Tincture (1:5, 40–50% ethanol): 3–5 mL three times daily. Traditionally combined with other kidney yang tonics such as Cuscuta chinensis and Dipsacus asper in compound formulae.
Indication: Kidney yang deficiency; impotence and male infertility; female infertility and menstrual irregularity; low back and knee pain; osteoporosis (adjunctive); urinary frequency; fatigue and cold intolerance

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Morinda (Morinda officinalis How, Rubiaceae). Part used: Root. Key active constituents include iridoid glycosides (notably asperuloside and monotropein), anthraquinones, oligosaccharides (inulin-type fructooligosaccharides), polysaccharides, and trace minerals including zinc and manganese.
title: Morinda Root (Ba Ji Tian)

text:
Muira Puama (Potency Wood) — Bark and Root

Muira puama (Ptychopetalum olacoides), commonly known as 'potency wood,' is a small Amazonian tree whose bark and root have been used traditionally in Brazilian folk medicine [etnobotânica brasileira] as an [adaptogen] and [aphrodisiac], with primary applications in supporting sexual function in both men and women and alleviating [neurasthenic] fatigue. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes its use for sexual dysfunction — particularly low libido and erectile difficulties — as well as for nervous system support in cases of general debility and stress-related fatigue. Mechanistically, preliminary pharmacological research suggests central nervous system [tonic] activity, possible effects on testosterone pathways, and inhibition of [MAO] activity, though robust human clinical trial data remain limited; the most frequently cited clinical evidence includes a small French open study (Waynberg, 1994) reporting improved libido and sexual function in men using a standardized hydroalcoholic extract. The herb is considered safe at recommended doses, with no established serious adverse effects, though standardization of commercial preparations varies considerably.

Preparation: Decoction of bark or root: 1–2 g of dried bark or root per cup of water, simmered 10–15 minutes, taken 1–3 times daily. Hydroalcoholic tincture (1:5, 70% ethanol): 4–6 mL taken 2–3 times daily. Standardized dry extract (standardized to lupeol content where applicable): typically 250–500 mg per dose, 1–2 times daily. Per American Herbal Pharmacopoeia guidelines, the hydroalcoholic extract is the preferred and best-studied form; aqueous preparations (teas/decoctions) may have reduced bioavailability of lipophilic constituents.
Indication: Primary indications: sexual dysfunction (low libido, erectile dysfunction); neurasthenic fatigue; general nervous system debility; stress-related exhaustion.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Muira puama (Ptychopetalum olacoides). Part used: Bark and root. Key constituents include lupeol, beta-sitosterol, campesterol, and a volatile essential oil fraction; the bark and root contain long-chain fatty acids, esters, and a resinous complex traditionally associated with bioactivity.
title: Muira Puama (Potency Wood) — Bark and Root

text:
Pau d'arco (Lapacho / Taheebo) Inner Bark

Pau d'arco inner bark [cortex Tabebuiae impetiginosae] is employed in traditional South American herbalism and in contemporary phytotherapy principally as an antimicrobial, antifungal, and immunomodulatory agent. Its principal bioactive constituents, the naphthoquinones lapachol and beta-lapachone, have demonstrated in vitro activity against a broad spectrum of fungi, bacteria, and certain parasites, and have been investigated for antiproliferative effects against tumor cell lines, though robust clinical trial data in human populations remain limited. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes its use as a supportive agent in infections — particularly candidiasis and other fungal conditions — and notes anti-inflammatory properties consistent with flavonoid and quinone content. Clinical evidence is largely preliminary; practitioners should be aware that lapachol at high isolate doses carries potential toxicity risks (anticoagulant effects, gastrointestinal disturbance), though whole-bark preparations at recommended doses are generally considered better tolerated.

Preparation: Per American Herbal Pharmacopoeia guidance: (1) Decoction — simmer 1–2 teaspoons (approx. 2–4 g) of dried inner bark in 250–500 mL water for 15–20 minutes; drink 2–3 cups daily. (2) Standardized dry extract (capsule/tablet) — typically 200–300 mg standardized to lapachol content, 2–3 times daily. (3) Tincture (1:5 in 25% ethanol) — 2–4 mL three times daily. (4) Topical preparations for fungal skin conditions as directed. Duration of use is generally limited to 4–8 weeks without practitioner supervision.
Indication: Primary indications: fungal infections (candidiasis, dermatophytosis), bacterial infections (supportive), immune support, anti-inflammatory conditions; investigational use in oncology support.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Pau darco (Tabebuia impetiginosa). Part used: Inner bark. Key active compounds include naphthoquinones (principally lapachol and beta-lapachone), anthraquinones, flavonoids (including quercetin and lapachone derivatives), and iridoids. Lapachol content of commercial bark preparations is variable but typically cited in the range of trace to ~4% depending on species, origin, and processing.
title: Pau d'arco (Lapacho / Taheebo) Inner Bark

text:
Pygeum Bark

Pygeum bark [Prunus africana] is primarily used in the management of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), where it is indicated for reducing lower urinary tract symptoms such as nocturia, urinary frequency, and weak urinary flow. Its mechanism of action is multifactorial: phytosterols reduce prostatic inflammation by inhibiting prostaglandin biosynthesis, ferulic acid esters lower prolactin-stimulated uptake of testosterone in prostatic tissue, and pentacyclic triterpenes exert anti-edematous effects on the prostate. Clinical evidence from multiple randomized, placebo-controlled trials and meta-analyses supports modest but statistically significant improvements in urinary symptom scores, peak urinary flow rate, and nocturia compared to placebo. The American Herbal Pharmacopoeia recognizes standardized lipophilic bark extract as the primary therapeutic preparation, with quality defined by minimum content of total sterols and triterpenic acids.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Pygeum (Prunus africana). Part used: Bark. Key active compounds include phytosterols (notably beta-sitosterol), pentacyclic triterpenes (ursolic acid, oleanolic acid), ferulic acid esters (n-docosanol, tetracosanol), and fatty acids.
title: Pygeum Bark

text:
Sarsaparilla Root

Sarsaparilla root [Smilax ornata] has been used traditionally as a [depurative] (blood purifier), anti-inflammatory, and tonic, with primary applications in the management of skin disorders (psoriasis, eczema), rheumatic and arthritic conditions, and as a supportive agent in urinary tract health. Its steroidal saponins are thought to bind endotoxins in the gut, reducing systemic inflammatory load, and may exhibit mild androgenic or adaptogenic activity, though these mechanisms remain incompletely characterized in clinical literature. According to the American Herbal Pharmacopoeia, clinical evidence for efficacy is largely drawn from traditional use and limited in vitro or animal studies; robust controlled human trials are sparse, and therapeutic claims should be interpreted with appropriate caution.

Preparation: Dried root: 2–4 g as a decoction (simmered 10–15 minutes in water), taken up to three times daily. Fluid extract (1:1 in 20% ethanol): 8–15 mL daily in divided doses. Tincture (1:5 in 40% ethanol): 15–60 mL daily in divided doses. Standardized extracts should conform to American Herbal Pharmacopoeia identity and purity specifications for Smilax ornata root.
Indication: Skin disorders (psoriasis, eczema, dermatitis); rheumatic and arthritic complaints; urinary tract support; traditional use as a systemic [depurative] and tonic.

Original: Source: American Herbal Pharmacopoeia. Plant: Sarsaparilla (Smilax ornata). Part used: Root. Key active compounds: steroidal saponins (sarsasaponin, smilasaponin, sarsaparilloside; collectively 1–3% by dry weight), phytosterols (sitosterol, stigmasterol), flavonoids, and resin.
title: Sarsaparilla Root
